explanations.answer: Raiders had killed all the older sons
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. The raiders who came into the camp with the Arabs had killed all the older sons, so the people of Jerusalem made Ahaziah king (2 Chronicles 22:1). He was the youngest son of Jehoram. I think he never pictured wearing that crown.

explanations.answer: The older sons turned down the throne
explanations.explanation: Nobody gets to turn anything down here, friend. The text says the raiders who had come into the camp with the Arabs had killed all the older sons (2 Chronicles 22:1). That left the youngest, Ahaziah, as the one the people of Jerusalem crowned. A throne can't be turned down by someone who isn't there.

explanations.answer: The older sons were away at war
explanations.explanation: War is close, but the text says something different. The raiders who came into the camp with the Arabs had killed all the older sons (2 Chronicles 22:1). That's why the people of Jerusalem made Ahaziah, the youngest, king. It's a heavy way to get a crown.

Yes, his mother. The text says she was his counselor in wickedness (2 Chronicles 22:3). Her name was Athaliah (2 Chronicles 22:2). Ahaziah walked in the ways of the house of Ahab with her voice in his ear.
No wife shows up in this passage, friend. The text says his mother was his counselor in wickedness (2 Chronicles 22:3). Her name was Athaliah (2 Chronicles 22:2). So the one in his ear was his mom.

A sister never comes up here, baker. The text says his mother was his counselor in wickedness (2 Chronicles 22:3). That's the voice Ahaziah listened to while he walked in the ways of the house of Ahab. Good guess, but it was his mom.

Destruction is right. The text says the house of Ahab counseled him "…to his destruction…" after his father died (2 Chronicles 22:4). Bad advice can sound friendly right up until the bill comes. Ahaziah followed it anyway.

I wish, friend, but no. The text says their counsel was "…to his destruction…" (2 Chronicles 22:4). It didn't lead anywhere good. That's the trouble with bad counselors, because they never say it up front.

Honor sounds nice, baker, but that's not where it went. The text says they counseled him "…to his destruction…" (2 Chronicles 22:4). Ahaziah followed their counsel, and it cost him. The house of Ahab was not handing out honor.

That's him. Ahaziah went with Joram to fight against Hazael king of Aram at Ramoth-gilead (2 Chronicles 22:5). Aram was the nation on the other side of that battle. Ahaziah followed the counsel he'd been given, and it took him into that fight.

Mesha is a different name from a different story, friend, and he doesn't show up here. At Ramoth-gilead the text names Hazael king of Aram as the one they fought (2 Chronicles 22:5). So the Arameans were across the field. Good thinking on a king's name, though.

Sennacherib doesn't show up in this passage, baker. The text says they went to fight against Hazael king of Aram at Ramoth-gilead (2 Chronicles 22:5). That's who stood on the other side. You picked a king, and it was a king, just a different one.

True. The text says "…the Arameans wounded Joram." (2 Chronicles 22:5). Joram was the king of Israel and the son of Ahab, and he came out of that fight hurt. Ahaziah had gone along, and the story keeps rolling from there.

Not false, friend. The text says "…the Arameans wounded Joram." (2 Chronicles 22:5). Joram, son of Ahab and king of Israel, got hurt at Ramoth-gilead. That wound is the reason for the visit that comes next.

explanations.answer: Goes down to Jezreel to visit him
explanations.explanation: Right on. The text says Ahaziah went down to Jezreel to visit Joram, because Joram had been wounded (2 Chronicles 22:6). Joram had returned to Jezreel to recover from the wounds the Arameans gave him. Sounds like a good friend, but hang on to that thought.

explanations.answer: Sends a letter wishing him well
explanations.explanation: A letter is a thoughtful idea, baker, but the text says something else. Ahaziah went down to Jezreel to visit Joram, because Joram had been wounded (2 Chronicles 22:6). No letter is mentioned. He went himself.

Jerusalem isn't where the text sends him, friend. It says Ahaziah went down to Jezreel to visit Joram, because Joram had been wounded (2 Chronicles 22:6). Joram had returned to Jezreel to recover. That's where Ahaziah headed.

Yes, from God. The text says "Ahaziah’s downfall came from God when he went to visit Joram." (2 Chronicles 22:7). It wasn't bad luck or bad timing. The same verse says that when he arrived, he went out with Joram to meet Jehu son of Nimshi.

Hazael was the king of Aram, the one they fought at Ramoth-gilead (2 Chronicles 22:5). But the text says Ahaziah's downfall "…came from God…" when he went to visit Joram (2 Chronicles 22:7). The visit is where it happened. Good thinking, since Hazael was in the story.

Elijah doesn't appear in this passage, baker. The text says Ahaziah's downfall "…came from God when he went to visit Joram." (2 Chronicles 22:7). That's the answer the verse gives. Elijah sat this one out.

That's the job. The LORD had anointed Jehu "…to destroy the house of Ahab." (2 Chronicles 22:7). And Ahaziah had been walking in the ways of that very house (2 Chronicles 22:3). When he arrived, he went out with Joram to meet Jehu.

Peace would've made for a calmer day, friend. But the text says the LORD had anointed Jehu "…to destroy the house of Ahab." (2 Chronicles 22:7). That's not a peace mission. Ahaziah went out with Joram to meet him.

Wall building is a fine job, baker, but the text gives a different one. It says the LORD had anointed Jehu "…to destroy the house of Ahab." (2 Chronicles 22:7). Samaria does come up later, when Ahaziah is hiding there (2 Chronicles 22:9). Rebuilding its walls isn't mentioned.

Rulers, yes. Jehu found the rulers of Judah and the sons of Ahaziah's brothers, who were serving Ahaziah (2 Chronicles 22:8). The text says he killed them. This part is heavy, so I'll just say it plainly.

Priests aren't named here, friend. The text says Jehu found "…the rulers of Judah and the sons of Ahaziah’s brothers…" who were serving Ahaziah (2 Chronicles 22:8). It's a heavy verse. The answer is rulers.

No prophets in this verse, baker. The text says Jehu found "…the rulers of Judah and the sons of Ahaziah’s brothers…" serving Ahaziah (2 Chronicles 22:8). It's a heavy moment, and rulers is the word the text uses.

True. Jehu looked for Ahaziah, and Jehu's soldiers captured him while he was hiding in Samaria (2 Chronicles 22:9). Then Ahaziah was brought to Jehu and put to death. It's a heavy moment in the story.

Not false, friend. The text says Jehu looked for Ahaziah, and his soldiers captured him while he was hiding in Samaria (2 Chronicles 22:9). Then Ahaziah was brought to Jehu. The hiding spot didn't hold.

explanations.answer: His grandfather Jehoshaphat sought the LORD
explanations.explanation: That's the reason they gave. They said, "He is the grandson of Jehoshaphat, who sought the LORD with all his heart." (2 Chronicles 22:9). Jehoshaphat was Ahaziah's grandfather. His grandfather's heart toward the LORD is why the burial happened.

explanations.answer: He had been the king of Judah
explanations.explanation: He was the king, baker, but that's not the reason given. They said, "He is the grandson of Jehoshaphat, who sought the LORD with all his heart." (2 Chronicles 22:9). The burial was because of his grandfather. The crown isn't mentioned.

explanations.answer: His mother Athaliah asked them to
explanations.explanation: Athaliah was his mother (2 Chronicles 22:2), but the text doesn't say she asked anyone anything here. The reason given is, "He is the grandson of Jehoshaphat, who sought the LORD with all his heart." (2 Chronicles 22:9). So it came down to his grandfather, friend.

Not quite, baker. The text says "…no one was left from the house of Ahaziah with the strength to rule the kingdom." (2 Chronicles 22:9). That qualifier matters, because it's about having the strength to rule. So this one is false.

False is right. The text says "…no one was left from the house of Ahaziah with the strength to rule the kingdom." (2 Chronicles 22:9). The verse is about having the strength to rule. It's a sober ending, friend.
